An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based)).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated simultaneous analyses in multiple collision types. With this capability, researchers were able to measure the efficiency and performance of various detectors, including the ATLAS tracking system, calorimeters, and external time projection chamber, in relation to their ionisation energy loss performance. Furthermore, they determined the characteristics of various forward detectors using pH2 data, evaluated the ATLAS detector's performance in relation to ALICE and CMS results, and derived measurements of the nuclear modification factor in relation to charged particle $p_T$ spectra and rapidity at central rapidities and in relation to proton-nucleon kinematic thresholds.

Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$. For certain matrix algebras, both $SO(N)$ and $SU(N)$, the series for $E_{ab}$ can be explicitly solved, and for all cases, the Hamiltonian $\hat H$ can be transformed to a commuting form, $\hat H_0$, by rescaling the deformation parameter by a factor of $[3]_q!/(48\theta^2)$, where $[3]_!= [1]_![2]_! [3]_! = (1-q^2)(1-q^3)(1-q^4)$, and $q$ is related to $\theta$. Rescaling has the effect of shifting the spectrum of $\hat H_0$ by a constant, $\epsilon_0 = \frac{1-q

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of a particular protein within tumor samples. Using the APLyso dataset as a model for privacy-preserved training, we simulated the creation of local models by different pathologists at different hospitals and compared the results of centrally-compiled and federated-learned models. Our analysis revealed that federated learning can produce models with comparable accuracy to traditionally trained models, despite not directly accessing the entire dataset. Additionally, federated learning offers the advantage of reducing the data storage demands associated with processing large medical image datasets.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 40 Gbit/s and a distance of 3.2 km in a underwater environment. The experiment reveals that laser intensity modulation combined with decision feedback equalization, without the need for a optical equalizer, results in dense, binary-sourced errors associated with the optical feedback connector, primarily caused by burst errors linked to air-water interfaces. To address this issue, an unequalized receiver is initially trained using an unequalized link without errors, allowing for error suppression during operational phases of the underwater system. Alternatively, an equalized receiver can be utilized to further enhance error suppression performance. The presented equalization technique yields substantial improvements in electrical and bit error rate performances, equivalent to an equivalent electrical SNR gain of approximately 6.5 dB and a corresponding bit error rate suppression of approximately 10^-6 to 10^-9, respectively. Consequently, decision feedback equalization can be effectively employed to suppress binary-sourced burst errors originating from an underwater connector within high-speed optical transmission systems. The proposed equalization methodology is also applicable to mitigate binary-sourced burst errors arising from other binary-disrupted environments, such as free space optical transmission systems.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as v3, and its associated magnitude in high-energy collisions between lead atoms at the LHC, operating at 5.02 TeV. These measurements were made for various collision settings and can be used to inform theoretical models of how these atoms interact. Additionally, researchers have built a simplified model to test how well they can predict the observed results. Interestingly, the model struggled to accurately forecast the observed fluctuations, particularly for lower multiplicity collisions. Furthermore, it appeared that hadronization played a key role in shaping the final form of matter produced from these collisions.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent.

The maintenance of consistent and accurate tables, devoid of anomalies and while considering dependencies, is crucial for supporting reliable decision-making. Prior research typically focuses on identifying flaws in data sets with defined constraints and dependencies, treating null values as a separate issue. In contrast, this study addresses inconsistencies arising from the interaction of null data with functional dependencies, especially in scenarios where missing information is inferred from the data's structure. We expand upon an existing approach to classify and manage such inconsistencies in a comprehensive way. Additionally, we apply these management techniques to real-world datasets with missing information, such as those found in the UCI machine learning repository.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the goal of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and can learn complex objects and task dynamics. In experiments,
we found that NDFs can successfully repeat demonstrated tasks on novel instances
from two object manipulation datasets, using only textural information. NDFs
outperformed a previous, rotation-symmetric object representation by using
sequence-descriptor matching, achieving this with fewer descriptors and better
performance on an entropy-trained model.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of a small low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch star, or multiple such stars, ejecta which did not significantly dynamo the cluster while it evolved. A bimodal carbon distribution was observed in Tononzintla 2 with both an blue and a red sequence, suggesting a relatively simple dynamo history for the cluster, and indicating that its stars probably acquired their carbon from external sources such as Type Type II supernovae or blue stellar remnant stars, and possibly low-mass AGB stars, as well. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration. However, as the archive continues to expand, the complexity in finding relevant proofs becomes apparent, much like a well-stocked library without clear organization. Addressing this issue, we propose a new approach to enhance the navigability of the archive by introducing a rating system that assigns a value to each proof based on its original research significance. We also explore ways to share modular components across unrelated projects, thereby reducing redundancy, and discuss the concept of proof inheritance. In addition, we present a setup theory framework to streamline the integration of newly developed foundational elements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these concepts by modifying existing entries, and we make our method publicly available through an open GitHub project.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models.

Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field, involving electromagnetic systems characterized by  
thin, expansive, and minutely featured particles that can also vary spatially,  
temporally, and linearly.  To tackle this intricacy, researchers need to employ a  
unified approach, integrating theoretical design and analysis methods, supported  
by an established framework.  Recent breakthroughs, facilitated by Generalized  
Sheet Transition Conditions in combination with surface susceptibilities,  
now enable designers to develop intricate metasurfaces, addressing longstanding  
challenges.  This paper delves into computational modeling of these complex  
structures through GSTC-susceptibility methodology and underscores its critical  
importance in the holistic design of metasurfaces, reviewing the evolution of  
recent frequency and time-domain computational methods.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This theoretical validation relies heavily on key concepts, including the formal orbital linearization theorem for formally integrable vector fields, the application of the blowing-up technique, and the application of the Sternberg-Chen theorem regarding formally equivalent smooth hyperbolic vector fields.

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision.

We have serendipitously identified a massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 gigaparsec, this feature exhibits a remarkable symmetry around the central host cluster, abiding by the principle of angular momentum conservation. It seems to be maintained by a delicate balance between gravitational pull and expansion, possibly induced by a series of supernovae-driven shocks and maintained through a process called the "ram pressure" from the intracluster medium. Its members exhibit a wide range of ages and are likely being stripped of their gas as they traverse the cosmic environment. The discovery of this Giant Arc not only deepens our understanding of the intricate interplay between host clusters and their surroundings but also may offer crucial insights into the vast web of filaments that make up the cosmic web.

While using photometry of stars to monitor the atmosphere and aerosols below has been around for some time, the technique is now being taken to the next level through the deployment of high-speed cameras capable of making numerous measurements per second in a very short window below which lies the aerosol layer in some of the world's premier astronomical sites. These highly advanced systems are essentially very high frequency aerosol radiometers that are providing unprecedented insights into the dynamics of the tropical stratospheric ozone layer in the Amazon region, as outlined in several recent scientific studies presented at the 2023 ALPA meeting in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues in a subsequent keypoint matching module. This approach has proven effective in pose estimation tasks where 5 degrees of freedom are limited. Nevertheless, applying such models to scenarios involving targets with poses of back-facing objects becomes challenging. In this paper, we present an innovative two-stage pipeline to estimate the pose of objects across all 6 degrees of freedom. Our proposed method, DeepHMap++, is an advancement of the DeepHMap framework, achieves pose regression by combining hierarchical object heatmap prediction with correspondence learning. Specifically, DeepHMap++ predicts hierarchical object heatmaps to capture robust object representations and employs a dual-path correspondence learning module guided by these heatmaps for reliable correspondence maps. The guidance from the object heatmap predictions enables the correspondence learning module to effectively construct correspondence vectors, thus facilitating pose estimation. Our experiments on the NYUv2 dataset validate the proposed method's performance, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on the benchmark protocol for 6D pose estimation tasks.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on sampling efficiency and free energy. It was discovered that methods rank into three categories based on their performance: methods outside the sampling efficiency collapse region suffer minimal sampling errors but incur significant computational costs per step; methods within the region's boundaries suffer greater errors but incur lesser costs; and methods within the region's center suffer immense errors but incur negligible costs. Furthermore, methods could be assigned efficiency scores relative to these regions. Additionally, it was established that some methods suffer immense sampling errors due to the non-commutativity of deterministic impulses and drifts, resulting in immense sampling inefficiencies in simulations of flexible molecules, thus rendering them futile for such purposes. It was also found that methods' susceptibility to sampling inefficiencies could be assessed via comparative tests, including an efficient implementation of Brownian motion. Ultimately, it was established that configurational molecular sampling could be resolved within the three sampling efficiency collapse regions, and some of these methods were found to be vastly more efficient than others, including current industry standards, thus rendering them significantly inferior in terms of efficiency.

Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start far too large to examine the detailed dynamics occurring near the merging black holes. Therefore, we need to bridge the gap between numerical relativity and general relativistic perturbation theory to fully understand their behavior. In this paper, we present purely 1D, non-relativistic simulations of how dark matter waves affect the environment surrounding binary black hole mergers. Our simulations cover a vast scale range by employing a precise mathematical formulation that accounts for both the discrete nature of dark matter and their overall fluid-like behavior under certain conditions. Notably, we observed that if the density of dark matter does not meet specific criteria, it can lead to a mismatch in angular momentum during the merger process, potentially leading to failures in post-merger simulations. Furthermore, we discovered that under certain conditions, the density of dark matter can lead to a significant heating effect on the environment surrounding the merging black holes, leading to a substantial increase in the amount of energy radiated as gravitational waves.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with angular velocity affecting the middle branch. A new model has been created to incorporate this effect. Through a direct approach, we establish the uniform stability of this model. Additionally, we demonstrate that an previously established benchmark model exhibits exponential stability.

Researchers utilized acoustic lenses composed of PMMA to increase the detection area of sensitive devices and improve resolution but discovered these lenses introduced image distortion. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world phenomena such as motion, the optical system and the color filter array, which combine to create relatively sharp raw images from motion-captured objects. Our model's deblurring demosaicking module is further modified by the introduction of a new element, which accounts for the optical system's point spread function (PSF) from the camera, in contrast to traditional deblurring methods that assume an idealized, static scene. Due to the inherent stability of this model's parameters, the problem of ill-posed deblurring can be effectively resolved even in the presence of motion-captured objects, as long as the camera's PSF is known. We demonstrate the proposed method's deblurring demosaicking module can be replaced with the introduced element in the generative model, thus incorporating the camera's PSF into the model. We utilize this model to train a deblurring demosaicking network that utilizes the model's prior to deblur and demosaick raw images affected by motion, without the need to simulate the process of converting scene and object motions into raw images. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study introduces an open source Python framework that utilizes background knowledge and observational data for the purpose of inferring causal relationships. This framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package, which executes a comprehensive causal discovery process to identify the causal interactions and the causal network structure among the variables, drawing from established methodologies including those from 'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg', in addition to pairwise algorithms like ANM. The framework is available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes, related to the sphere's speed, size, and the forces at play, are presented. A notable finding from our research, conducted in both gravity-dominated and inertia-dominated gravity regimes, was the discovery of a universal threshold, centered around a critical Koehler number, that determines if the seal forms successfully, thus revealing a previously unidentified intermediate regime in the water entry process.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied the typical superpotential and deformation terms in Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity effective field theories and found that, under most conditions, the superpotential induces a universal vacuum expectation value for the axion-dilaton field. This breaks the $SL(2,S)$ duality symmetry in a way that allows for potential quantum gravity signatures. We investigated the conditions under which this breakdown occurs and explored the implications for the characteristics of duality domains. A key finding was that non-zero values for generalized theta-terms would signify the presence of charged black holes and macroscopic field gradients in its vicinity. We also examined the potential effects of these phenomena on cosmic microwave background gravitational waves produced during cosmic inflation.

Mobile device owners frequently require running multiple time-sensitive applications concurrently, often collaborating with unverified online services on the same device. To address this recurring issue, researchers have introduced hardware that allows for sequential execution of programs, where each has temporary, full control over the processor and associated peripherals. Although they utilized cryptographic signatures and historical data to validate the origin of programs and build trust in developers' intentions, these approaches rely on devices' creators or program developers. We propose an alternative approach, called Minimizing Trust with Exclusively-Used Physically-Isolated Hardware, or MITEXPU, which eliminates the need to verify programs' creators or intentions. Instead, MITEXPU utilizes hardware that ensures each program's safe and uninterrupted access to the processor and related components, resulting in significant performance improvements, including 1.3 to 2 times faster CPU access, and reduced system entry/exit by 40 to 80 percent.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(1)$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an sample and sample efficiency $O(\epsilon^{-2})$. The above results are derived for the general case and deterministic value-based algorithms in MDPs with finite states and actions.

We uncover an unselectable version of the box game paradox, featuring players making remarkably accurate predictions of unknown real numbers without access to relevant information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the requirement of choice in solving the classic problem and examines alternative configurations of the game.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular benefit, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby confirming their potential utility in quantum communication and computation applications.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to achieve desired tidal volumes for both patients.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from external images is a highly intricate task due to variations in appearance, shadows cast by surrounding structures from the imaging and from moving muscles in the esophagus. These factors present significant obstacles to accurately detecting and outlining tumors in external images. To overcome these difficulties, we designed an innovative network called esophageal tumor segmentation network (DDAUnet) that integrates spatial attention mechanisms into a Dense Unet architecture. By leveraging features from multiple scales and prioritizing tumor-relevant information, our model can effectively manage variations seen in such images. Through the use of dilated convolution and an attention-reinforced U-shape network, our (DDAUnet) is capable of capturing fine details and preserving the continuity of tumor boundaries. By pretraining our model on a comprehensive chest CT dataset and fine-tuning it on a limited esophageal CT dataset, our results indicate that the DDAUnet achieves high levels of accuracy in identifying and outlining tumors in such images, with metrics of 0.833 for Dice Similarity Coefficient, 3.313 mm for Hausdorff Distance, 1.629 mm for Average Surface Distance, and 94.125% for Pixel Accuracy.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving accurate well placement and tracking during drilling requires understanding the uncertainty in log interpretation. A statistical approach has been utilized in this study to assess the data noise in logs and calculate the resulting covariance. The impact of various sources of log noise is assessed, and the resulting probability distributions are employed in a machine learning classification method to assess their effect on training data. The resulting ensemble-based classifier yields not only class predictions, but also an indicator of prediction reliability. The method was successfully applied in a case study, where the ensemble-based classification method was able to accurately predict water and oil zones, along with quantifying the associated risks. The method's ability to guide well trajectory during drilling in response to these estimates and their uncertainties has been demonstrated. The code associated with the ensemble-based method along with its application in logging interpretation is freely accessible on a public repository. The potential for integrating this method into real-time geosteering guidance systems has been shown, along with the ability to generate prediction intervals to visualize the associated risks in well logs. The importance of considering log data noise and the resulting uncertainty in logging interpretation has been highlighted, with the ability to guide well trajectory during drilling highlighted. The method's versatility in handling various logging techniques and machine learning classifiers has been demonstrated, with the ability to generate prediction intervals to visualize the associated risks in well logs.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability to low-resource scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, but also highlight significant improvements in languages with limited annotations, such as Basque.

We extend the use of tropical methods to counting in arithmetic problems, such as enumerating objects in higher-dimensional spaces using values from specific algebraic structures, over fields that have been modified to have special values, such as plane quartics with specific tangent properties as a reference. We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. We express obstacles to counting these curves and their associated tangencies by altering the structure of these curves and their starting properties, focusing on edges and how they are affected. We show that by understanding how these curves and their starting properties change when modified, we can calculate the relative importance of these curves when counting them using these specific algebraic structures, or "GW-multiplicity". This allows us to verify a previously proposed mathematical relationship involving these curves and their counts. This verification relies on a deeper understanding of how the algebraic structures of these fields are related, especially when these fields are modified to have special values, or "residue fields".

Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, with some still unexplored, complicating such analyses. To resolve this, researchers used a genetic algorithm to identify and verify multiple Ta$_2$O$_5$ phases to understand their stability and electronic characteristics. These simulations considered different environments, oxygen levels, and local magnetic behaviors. Notably, they discovered that Ta$_2$O$_5$ within its B phase exhibits a metallic state even in its ideal state. Additionally, they discovered that defect Ta$_2$O$_5$ displays a dielectric characteristic typical of its defect form. Ultimately, the nucleic algorithm identified and validated a more stable defect B phase Ta$_2$O$_5$ material exhibiting a dielectric characteristic.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources.

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting fraudulent credit card transactions and (2) detecting biased news articles promoting hate.

Compared to baseline models, introducing the algorithm leads to a significant reduction in the number of events that require human judgment by a factor of at least 50, while sustaining high precision and minimizing the number of missed detections.

We also discuss the implications of our approach from multiple perspectives, including human intuition, computational efficiency, and legal compliance.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods.

Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm, illustrating its use in deriving formulas by utilizing the underlying proof of correctness.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2002.06068, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, especially their role in resolving issues related to infinite complexity values. Our theoretical investigations are supplemented by numerical simulations, showcasing the emergence of distinct optimal paths in both state and operator complexity scenarios. These findings also pave the way for further exploration into generalized models, including those involving many-body systems.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances.

Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties and minimum standard deviation required to potentially identify a hypothetical eighth planet. The model considers a scenario where this planet is equally likely to orbit the solar system anywhere between 500 AU and 1000 AU. However, the model assumes the planet is uniformly distributed within this range, which doesn't fully capture our limited visibility. By integrating the model's model over possible distances, a potential indicator is calculated as a ratio of the standard deviation in gravitational mass estimation for the solar system's outer region to the estimated minimum standard deviation. If this ratio is less than one, our present measurements and observations are sufficiently precise to potentially confirm or rule out the existence of the hypothetical Planet X. The model yields a surprising and perhaps unsettling finding: the gravitational mass estimations are so imprecise that the ratio is less than one for as little as 400 AU.

Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables enriched TM with monolingual data yield higher recall rates; secondly, the cross-lingual memory retrieval mechanism enables more relevant memories to be obtained. Experimental outcomes show that the proposed method achieves substantial performance gains over TM-augmented NMT baselines in both low and high coverage scenarios.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data and found no statistical significance for the low-variance circles identified by Penrose and others. A new approach to assessing the significance of these circles considers the typical thickness of the data pixels and the realistic range of circle sizes, both of which differ from the conditions used in the original analysis. Additionally, a straightforward method to determine the expected circle thickness leads to a contradiction with the observed circle thickness. We also discovered that increasing the circle density to match or exceed the likelihood of overlapping Hawking points results in low-variance circles similar to those found. Furthermore, a simpler way of calculating the expected circle diameter leads to it being larger than the observable universe.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing a Yamabe flow based on fractional curvature and demonstrating the existence of mild solutions. The current research expands on that study by establishing the convergence of the flow under certain data conditions within a broader framework. The new results are derived from an approach simplified by Struwe in his book.

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011).

Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Filtering tackles a common issue in current recommendation systems, namely the scarcity of data and the presence of multiple, data-sparse domains simultaneously. In order to tackle this challenge, users' multi-faceted preferences must be considered, taking into account their diverse interests across different contexts. However, the latent, multi-aspect nature of user preferences and the isolated behavior users sometimes exhibit in separate domains, presents a significant obstacle to effective recommendation. In order to tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel, multi-sparse-domain collaborative filtering approach, namely ESAPL, which leverages user's comprehensive aspect-preferences to bridge the user's isolated behavior. By representing users' multi-faceted preferences as separate, graph-based representations of their interactions with goods across different categories, ESAPA learns the hidden, multi-aspect preferences and utilizes them to tackle data sparsity issues via cross-domain mutual learning. In order to further enhance the accuracy of ESAPL's recommendations, we integrate a graph neural network to tackle the users' low-dimensional hidden attributes. The experimental results confirm the efficacy of ESAPL in producing highly accurate recommendations.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,033 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific generalization capabilities across several major datasets. Our findings indicated that using the MRIQC pipeline without preprocessing yielded the best results, outperforming its fully processed counterpart, and demonstrated excellent generalization on unseen data without the need for retraining or fine-tuning, however, some datasets did demonstrate improved performance after fine-tuning with their own quality control data.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel as primary memory and persistent storage accessible by user-level applications. Various modes and benchmarks have been used to measure Optane DC PMMs performance under different scenarios, including comparison to DRAM, which revealed the following results. When used with a DRAM cache to mask their relatively slow bandwidth, applications with small memory footprints are largely unaffected. Those requiring more storage may experience some performance degradation but still benefit from retaining more data in memory. In file system benchmark tests, user-level applications utilizing Optane DC PMMs as storage outperformed traditional block device methods in most cases, with the largest improvements seen in data-intensive applications.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded by incorporating a recurrent structure, which is then used in designing a state-dependent function to facilitate a group of agents on a circular path to converge at a single point. The paper includes a theoretical proof of convergence and a practical verification of this process in a real-world setting.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials through spin-polarized and unpolarized calculations, revealing that they adopt the same cubic SmAl3-type structure and behave as metallic systems. It was discovered that the Gd and Cm atoms in GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds respectively contribute significantly to the total magnetic moment via their core spins. Additionally, the GdxCm1-xSn compounds exhibit inhomogeneous distribution of up and down spins due to the competing Gd-Cm 4f electrons. Variations in the total magnetic moment of GdxCm1-xSn compounds with changing composition can be managed by adjusting the Gd and Cm atomic ratios. These results suggest that the GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn materials exhibit strong potential for use in metallic spintronic devices.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of powers of its elements, taken from a particular generating set. In this study, a specific variant of OGS relevant to the symmetric group S_n is explored, and a corresponding form for the finite Coxeter group of the B_n type is proven. Furthermore, a basic generating sequence (BGS) formulation for the B_n type is established, and the corresponding expression representation is also obtained.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2} h^{-3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced scattering will become a notable source of noise in SN Ia data, potentially hindering local Hubble diagram measurements at $z \sim 0.1$ with the DESIA and Euclid surveys.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included. 

The concluding chapter covers the pathwise approach.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process.

MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness.

In this research, we explore the properties of a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$, as well as its corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic framework for generating functions and symbolic evaluation functions, allowing us to derive $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. Our findings demonstrate intriguing connections with circulant matrices and Galois fields, while showcasing the potential for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ to be applied in computationally efficient contexts.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to extract rotational signals from observational data sets of high-activity M dwarfs. Our research focused on FS Aur and TV Cnc, representing typical high-activity Kolb Class 2.5 and 3 stars, respectively. We found that minimizing the residual rotational signal requires carefully selecting lines based on their equivalent widths. When analysing the results, we considered the line lists in terms of $\log$ $S(f_{rot})/S_{spec, res}$, where $S(f_{rot})$ represents the power spectrum at the rotation frequency and $S_{spec, res}$ denotes the mean observed spectral resolution. We observed that using line lists comprising both strong and weak lines results in the most efficient extraction of the rotational signal. To further investigate this, we conducted a/jitter-line$ relationship study on FS Aur and TV Cnc, still in its early stages. Notably, we found no significant correlation between stellar properties and lines used for deconvolution, as well as between activity and lines for these two stars. To address this, future high activity studies should sample

This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a hasty data collection process in a Wireless Sensor Network, ensuring high-speed performance and superior efficiency. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is discussed, employing a bidirectional approach to accurately measure the quality of communication links. Secondly, a quality-based sectoring strategy is examined, organized in a hierarchical structure with the aim of dividing the network into sectors to optimize data collection. A simulation study utilizes TCPnet as a performance metric and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed techniques, resulting in significantly reduced mission completion times and precise quality measurements.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into five groups based on how they model context: traditional R-CNN types that skip context, CNNs that focus on parts, and those that ignore scene context like ENet, bases for scoring proposals, and re-ranking.
Our analysis of performance and proposal context led to the selection of an envelope network for this challenge.
Including context information from different parts of images helps improve detection performance on the data set.
However, for some models adding context has limited benefit due to their reliance on anchor boxes.
Our best results used proposals with low context but strong confidence.
This study EnANet stands out as the first proposal enriched with context using an ENet network base, leading to comparison advantages over other models using different architectures.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube and exhibit partial independence, subject to monotonicity constraints. Notably, we establish new bounds for functions subject to the convexity condition, along with new results under the framework of subgaussian concentration. Furthermore, our bounds incorporate the influence of Lipschitz and Hamiltonian conditions. These new inequalities have practical applications in analyzing algorithms for balanced flow and balanced cut problems under the assumption of partial independence.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$.

This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function.

We've established recently, much like our work on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed from a novel, deformed form of the Poisson brackets.  Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}.  With the deformed algebra in hand, we derive the first Casimir invariant in this paper.  Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating its capability to recommend accurate and relevant entities to users using the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys.
