MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering systems have gained significant attention in inverse problems due to their ability to accurately model complex light transport phenomena, which cannot be easily reversed. The concept of differentiable shadow computation has long been established, and its basic principle can be reversed by simply reordering operations in a shadow calculation algorithm. The issue arises from the fact that shadow calculations often involve nonlinear operations such as area-based integrations and binary masking, which cannot be directly reversed in a differentiable manner. As an alternative solution, we present a novel algorithm called Shadow Reversal, which achieves a more efficient reversal operation with minimal performance loss compared to the forward simulation. The problem of shadow filling in the reversed computation can be effectively addressed by modifying the Jacobian application in the integrator, rather than relying on the traditional approach of modifying the integrand, and thereby avoiding unnecessary additional computations, such as solving linear systems. The proposed algorithm is particularly beneficial in scenarios with opaque objects, where the computation of visible flags can be significantly optimized, and the necessary visible flags in Shadow Reversal can be calculated on object vertices, and marked as either fully visible or completely occluded, and this optimization can be further simplified, as objects in many applications do not self-occlude, thus avoiding the need for ray tracing, and significantly reducing computational costs, such as in scene deblur, hyperpainting, and high dynamic range (HDR) reconstruction problems.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning tools are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even in scenarios where new bathymetry data is unavailable. Moreover, by utilizing a generative model, the fast solver can generate physically realistic predictions of flow velocities, thereby avoiding the unreasonably high flow velocities that may arise from traditional neural network-based solutions.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an n by n symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries conforming to specific conditions, our primary finding establishes that under additional assumptions, the matrix converges to the standard scaled Wigner matrix in operator norm. However, in the absence of additional assumptions, we prove a broader convergence result for the empirical distribution of eigenvalues to the semi-circular distribution in probability with respect to the Kolmogorov metric. Furthermore, this implies convergence in the sense of moments, given that higher order moment information in the standard scaled Wigner case directly correlates with non-crossing partition data. In contrast, our paper demonstrates that a broader range of distributional information is required for general entries. This, combined with an analysis of the Stieltjes transform, enables derivation of explicit formulae for the first two moments of the empirical distribution of eigenvalues.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, seamless video flow, and audio synchronization. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 30 degrees and efficiently redirecting both plane and focused ultrasound beams at 7.1 MHz. These designs were successfully manufactured using two-photon polymerization and experimentally validated, demonstrating reflection coefficients of over 65% and a broad bandwidth of more than 70kHz for both beam redirection applications.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components, as it enables the introduction of new, structured elements and significant changes in the virtual world, and it tracks transfers in performance and transferable knowledge. As such, L2Explorer represents a crucial step forward in advancing reinforcement learning research, and we invite researchers to build upon this foundation and develop innovative solutions to real-world problems.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization for specific quasiperiodic patterns, representing a new phenomenon known as reentrant delocalization. Additionally, we observe that as disorder increases, this reentrant phenomenon becomes more prominent.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10}M_{\odot}$, there was no significant difference in the color behavior between the central and outer regions. Conversely, at stellar masses greater than $10^{10}M_{\dot}$ a significant difference emerged. Notably, galaxies with NUV$r > 0.6$ in their central regions showed an increase in frequency as stellar mass increased, in line with observations of the star formation main sequence. In contrast, galaxies with NUV$r < 0.6$ displayed a declining trend. These findings indicate that bulge growth is a key factor in shaping the star formation main sequence at the high mass end.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence configurations into programs to ensure their correct operation within the defined model. To demonstrate the applicability of our approach, we develop several reordering bugs that would not occur with total store ordering and can be incorporated into mainstream codebases. Lastly, we examine the feasibility of implementing a prototype system that employs a custom memory model, utilizing both coherence-based and program-based self-invalidation and self-downgrade mechanisms.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to consecutive integer sequences.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $B^{H}_{t}+f_{t}$ denoted by $X_{t}$ for all $t$ in $[0,1]$. It is proven that if $H$ is greater than $1/2$, and $f$ has bounded variation, then the image measure $\mu^{X}$ has a density that is $C^{1}$-continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, implying $\mu^{X}$ will also have a non-empty interior. For $H$ in the interval $(1/3,1/2)$, this result holds provided $f$ is a Holder continuous function with exponent $\alpha$ greater than $2H-1$. Furthermore, if $H$ is less than $1/2$, and $f$ has infinite variation, such as being Holder continuous with exponent $\alpha$ greater than $2H$, then $\mu^{X}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This last property indicates that $\mu^{X}$ has a non-zero density on a set of non-zero Lebesgue measure.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on canonical transformation, applicable to both classical and quantum mechanics. A single variational parameter is employed to obtain the system's Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, and Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The result is an effective Morse potential, whose solutions provide approximate values for the system's energy levels' splitting. This approach highlights the effectiveness of the VAMPOLE method in capturing non-linear resonance behavior, a capability that traditional variational principles lack.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics indicating symptoms of COVID-19 patients, which can hint at their likelihood of requiring intensive care. Although we lack the capability to quantify these features, ourL-19XrayIntensiveIcon图表示需要入住重症监护室.

We suspect that certain features, which we cannot fully describe, may be associated with a patient's need for intensive care. To test this hypothesis, we constructed a hypothesis model based on chest X-ray images, which we then used to train a machine learning model.

Our initial model achieved a high accuracy of 91% in predicting intensive care needs. However, we believe this model is missing some crucial information, which we cannot visualize. To address this limitation, we constructed more complex neural network models, incorporating attention mechanisms and graph neural networks.

These advanced models yielded varying degrees of accuracy, which improved upon our initial model. Specifically, we found that an attention mechanism model achieved the highest accuracy of 95%. It is possible that there are additional, currently unknown features in X-ray images that are relevant to intensive care admission.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. We've experimented with multiple training and prediction methods including cross-domain techniques, as well as introducing an efficient yet straightforward approach for frame selection. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing benchmark models with a significant margin of 11% improvement.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures the content-based parallel processing capability often referred to as AMIPS, which blends features of AIPS and MIPS. The proposed system was based on the AIPS architecture but capable of floating point operations, then applied to real-time image processing on an Ubuntu Linux-based FPGAbot. Successfully achieving its intended function, the Content Addressable Parallel Processor demonstrated efficient use of on-chip resources while delivering improved performance. When compared to its non-CAM counterpart and the host CPU using OpenCV, our design exhibited a 2.87-fold reduction in processing time for the same image, totaling 39.02 milliseconds.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching, a process where their mass is being formed into massive disks by gas that maintains their overall symmetry. Furthermore, we propose that these galaxies are undergoing a critical transition phase, in which bulges are being created within these massive quiescent disks. Specifically, we observed that the inner regions of these galaxies are experiencing a star formation quenching process induced by a lack of angular momentum and self-regulation of supernovae, resulting in the rapid collapse of gas into bulges while the extended disks remain alive and star-forming. We conclude that massive quiescent disks hosting dense bulges are the natural progression of these galaxy systems.

We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1709.08218. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass hierarchy and absolute mass estimates from neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Our revised analysis significantly surpasses the initial analysis and demonstrates that the UTZ theory of flavour remains a coherent and well-supported framework. Additionally, our team released open-source MCMC code and comprehensive UTZ parameter sets for both its primary and secondary contributions, accessible at the provided URLs.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device, prompting an inquiry into the legal obligation of the individual to provide the passcode. To answer this question, the article draws on first principles, as well as the 3rd and 4th Amendments to the US Constitution, to establish the passcode's status as a form of speech and thought, thereby rendering compelled disclosure as a violation of these constitutional protections. The article's proposed solution, rooted in 'age-old' legal doctrines, suggests that the court can compel the individual to reveal the passcode to a third party who, in turn, can verify the accuracy of the passcode. Furthermore, the article's theoretical framework leads to the conclusion that compelling a passcode to a third party under these doctrines aligns with the spirit of the 3rd and 4th Amendments. The article's findings are illustrated with the example of Subpoena Apple, a judge-driven method that utilizes Apple's iCloud to recover a lost or stolen iPhone without a passcode, via the device's Erase iPhone feature.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal process occurring within a nearby star, HD 20794, as it undergoes rapid changes in brightness. Although the system appears stable on the outside, the presence of an eccentric planet engulfs the star's outer layers, potentially altering the system's dynamics. By analyzing the star's varying line profiles and activity indicators, a model is proposed suggesting the planet's interaction may be responsible for the observed changes in angular momentum transport, which could either support or challenge the angular momentum engineering theory.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation is attributed to the scarcity of labeled data available for training in such situations. To address this challenge, our goal is to develop a generalizable system capable of accurately detecting false news across both established and newly emerging events on social media. We introduce a novel Meta Fake News Detection approach, the first of its kind to incorporate emergent events, by utilizing transfer learning and few-shot learning techniques. Our method leverages a pre-trained ensemble model to classify newly emerging events and introduces the Meta Neural Process network to efficiently adapt to these events with minimal labeled data. The results indicate that our method outperforms current baselines in detecting false news in both established and newly emerging events.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. Furthermore, we outline our future objectives and objectives for the data analysis and interpretation stages of the SDSS-V.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates when working with high-dimensional categorical data, leading to a model that is overly complex and fails to identify relevant features for each category. To address this issue, we introduce two techniques that transform categorical data into dense numerical representations while preserving the model's ability to identify relevant features, allowing us to leverage effective and robust sparse models. Mathematical analysis confirms that our transformations maintain mathematical equivalence to the original Group Lasso problem, while empirical results show significant improvements in both solution quality and computational efficiency when combined state-of-the-art solvers.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations tend to be预先 aligned in the same direction. Taking advantage of this initial setup, researchers can streamline the process of aligning overlapping images in panoramic stitching projects. In accordance with this approach, the restrictive parameters for these images can be predetermined as perpendicular to the axis of the cameras. As a result, the number of unknown variables in this problem is significantly reduced, thereby improving computational performance. Building upon this principle, the objective function is formulated to maximize the compatibility of these images, considering only those features that satisfy this constraint. The purposeful function proposed in this research can be efficiently solved using iterative methods, yielding a computationally feasible and computationally efficient solution within a reasonable timeframe. Moreover, the algorithm presented in this study demonstrates robustness against imperfect preprocessing steps and scenes containing objects unrelated to the predetermined parameters. In comparison studies, the proposed method exhibits superior runtime performance and produces high-quality outputs with minimal user input and post-processing requirements, despite competing with established techniques including those employing globally optimal solutions.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from a healthy marmoset model to diseased marmoset models treated with a dopaminergic drug. These results demonstrate the potential of data-driven biophysical models to elucidate the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease and support the development of effective therapeutic strategies.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-800 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a relationship that holds true across different stages of infrared luminosity and supermassive black hole mass. Several areas within our targets exhibit signs of active galactic nuclei powered by ultra/luminous infrared galaxies. Furthermore, we observed the presence of highly active star forming regions as well as gas outflows triggered by active galactic nuclei within several of our targets. Upcoming studies will

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing the Co-Training method to accelerate the training process for Convolutional Neural Networks in weather classification.
Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by outperforming other methods in terms of accuracy.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy input sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal connections. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Neural Networks. The DPCRN model features two parallel RNN structures, one processing the primary input and the other processing an inverted bit-mask of the primary input. These networks share the same hidden layers and only their bias terms differ. Experiments using the LibriSpeech dataset demonstrate that the DPCRN model outperforms both a standard Convolution Recurrent Network and a previous Dual-Path RNN model in terms of speech separation performance.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference in turn-around radii probability distribution means, while $\Lambda$CDM and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $7\sigma$ difference in the same metric. Furthermore, adding the effect of massive neutrinos allows $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV to be differentiated by $6\sigma$ difference in virial radii and $12\sigma$ difference in turn-around radii.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms. By applying time-dependent strong coupling changes in sequence, we can transform initially independent, mixed states into a genuinely entangled whole. Our protocol works by first entangling the uncorrelated systems through strong coupling strong coupling interactions and then maintaining the generated entanglement by taking advantage of the uncorrelated systems' interactions. Notably, our method does not require measuring or controlling the optical fields within the cavities.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics. Using a cubic model, we examine how the nonlinear interaction influences an anti-de Sitter black hole's mass, entropy, and heat capacity. Our study finds that the nonlinear interaction changes the relationship between heat capacity and shadow radius for both large and small black holes, providing a new method for classifying black holes based on shadow imaging and interferometry. Additionally, the difference in this relationship with temperature can be seen through their shadows, offering a potential method for observing this effect through shadow observations.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our approach aims to
train a role-specific model on minimal data that specifies the desired feature.
To accomplish this, we utilize minimal data to: a) instruct the model on its
assigned role, utilizing explicit instructions for persona or abstract summaries
for safety, and b) generate human-human dialogue with the desired role through
fine-tuning with explicit prompts or role-specific models and then filtering the
results for quality, and finally, we evaluate our role-specified dataset and model
across multiple scenarios including persona-based dialogue, safety-enforced
conversations, enforcing specific roles, and lastly, we discuss potential areas
for future research.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value in enhancing viewport prediction models.
Therefore, to leverage this potential, a new dataset including navigation data
was created and incorporated into a new proposal for viewport prediction by
integrating this additional information with an existing model based on visual
importance. The combined approach, known as NAV-IAN, was shown to outperform
other methods through comprehensive evaluation results.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
