It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

The provided article introduces an Itô-Wentzell type formula tailored to accommodate paths with α-Hölder regularity of $\alpha$ within the interval $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}]$. Additionally, it expands on prior work by R. Castrequini and P. Catuogno concerning Young integrals, as well as research by C. Keller and J. Zhang on rough paths.

In the context of federated learning, a significant challenge arises when client data displays considerable statistical heterogeneity. This paper explores the application of random walk theory to tackle this issue. Our approach enables each client to generate a random walk sequence based on their local data and their interaction with neighboring clients. This allows for the creation of isolated learning processes for each client, despite the variation in data statistics. A key innovation of our proposed method is the use of random walk lengths that increase over time, which helps clients learn from larger data subsets while maintaining balance between model performance and computational costs. Additionally, our framework facilitates clients with higher-quality data to contribute more significantly to the final model. The proposed method achieves remarkable results in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and computational costs when compared to existing approaches for heterogeneous data.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of multistability in rotating turbulent flows. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that significant geostrophic vortical structures can be superimposed onto the wave turbulence spectrum without disrupting its underlying dynamics.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who received mental health treatment against those who did not.  It discovered that mental health treatment as part of probation can decrease recidivism by 8.4% among offenders who commit non-violent crimes.  The results suggest mental health treatment can be more cost effective than incarceration.  Additionally, the findings indicate successful crime prevention through mental health treatment has benefits extending beyond the justice system.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed label. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting by leveraging the agreement between separate training samples. Experimentation on multiple medical datasets, including Cardiac MRI, ATLAS, and私产MRI, demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique in achieving high levels of accuracy with limited labeled data.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve four distinct modules, each housed in its own card, with two of these cards containing 8 Intel Pseudo Assets (XQPAs) and two containing 4 each. This design will require significant high-speed data transfer capabilities, ultimately necessitating under 224 gigabits per second of bandwidth from the XQPAs to the main processor card. This final card will be based on an Intel Xilinx UltraScale+ processor running within 400 nanoseconds latency. To develop the jFEX hardware system, a prototype board has been designed and constructed. This prototype board demonstrates the feasibility of this system architecture but currently relies on customized firmware due to limitations with the commercial drivers for the XQPA cards.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, demonstrating its superiority
through clear preferences and outstanding results on quantitative assessment metrics.
ANR enabled significantly natural and smooth character animation within a virtual
environment.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result by Newton and Raftery (1994) fits into this framework. Additionally, we provide GMLEs and their corresponding standard errors for both clustered data and sampling with unequal selection probabilities and these estimators are tested through a simulation study.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications and numerous solvers now generate proofs in this same  
format. As the next step in further improvement, the current format is being  
thoroughly examined to incorporate the latest features while also looking at past  
extensions to the DPLL(LA) proof format. This comprehensive assessment is being  
conducted with the goal of creating a more versatile and standardized system that  
is both backward compatible and capable of supporting a diverse set of theories,  
which in turn, has the potential to greatly streamline the development of future  
extensions. This work is being conducted with the goal of creating a more versatile  
and standardized DPLL(LA) proof format that will benefit the entire community in the  
next decade by establishing a common foundation for the verification efforts across  
a diverse set of systems.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER).

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms.

Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. Moreover, the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ spectrum, where $\rho^0(1450)$ cannot contribute due to Bose-Einstein statistics, is accounted for by an $S$-wave contribution alone.  The theoretical estimates of branching fractions and/or direct $CP$ asymmetries for $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome. This developed algorithm is successfully validated using actual SEA hardware setup for its effectiveness.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been considered. Additionally, we explored whether lattice model transitions relate to the behavior of continuum field theory at its stable charged fixed points, particularly for 2 color gauge group SU(Nc=2) where we found some evidence that charged critical behaviors occur when there are more flavors (Nf > Nf*) of scalar field, and that this value of Nf lies within the range 20 to 40.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to exhibit the k = n^2/3 relationship.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts.

Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe that a bar forms in the center within one billion years, along with spiral arms composed of 2, 3, and 4-armed patterns. These features persist for at least 3 billion years in our simulations. However, we find that a bar won't develop if the galaxy's disk has a radial scale longer than 2.6 kiloparsecs. A compact bulge also prevents bar formation, as predicted. Our findings also indicate that a bar contributes to the maximum rotation curve in a galaxy's central regions due to its shape and orientation.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a high degree of impact on how galaxy mergers unfold. These magnetic fields hinder the development of gravitational instability in galaxy discs, limiting the creation of stars and causing more pronounced features in the generated star formation patterns. As a result, more stars are produced during the starburst period and fewer remain in the galaxy's halo. These fields also compress the galaxy discs, creating thicker patterns in the formed stars. During galaxy disc interactions, greater energy is transferred to the galaxy's internal structure and to magnetic fields outside, causing more pronounced changes in the galaxy's overall shape, especially in its halo.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work has been done on addressing the challenge of domain shifts. Growsdiar proposes to tackle low-resource domain shifts in GEC through the use of meta-learning. Specifically, we employ a few-shot domain adaptation strategy, where the source domain serves as the base for learning model parameters capable of efficiently adapting to new domains with minimal pseudo data. By framing domain adaptation in the GEC context as a series of continual meta-learning tasks, we can leverage standard multi-shot meta-learning algorithms to update the model parameters, thereby enhancing its ability to generalize to new domains. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Growsdiar in handling domain shifts in GEC, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-shot experiments and substantial gains in low-resource single-shot experiments.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have long gone unstudied. To understand how rounding affects variable counts, this study derives the probability distribution for a non-negative random variable $X$ based on its rounded value. Given that $⌊nX⌋$ adheres to a specific probability law and $n$ is sufficiently large, we determine the probability that the rounded variable equals a specific non-negative integer and provide an approximate formula. An approximate method is also developed for calculating the mean of the distribution. These advancements enable using average data to infer the probability distribution, mean, and median of an underlying random variable. By applying this method to several datasets, the study derives estimated parameters for the underlying distribution.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal material GdInO3, which has a hexagonal structure along the c-axis. Using X-ray diffraction, they found that GdInO3 behaves as a normal perovskite, with two adjacent Gd3+ ions forming a centered honeycomb framework in the ab-plane. By conducting DC and AC susceptibility and specific heat measurements, the researchers determined that GdInO3 exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior, with a Néel temperature of approximately 17.1 K. The magnetic properties of GdInO3 can be effectively explained by a centered honeycomb Heisenberg model with two exchange interactions. Furthermore, specific heat analysis revealed a two-kink structure in the reduced specific heat curve at the Néel temperature and a Gd3+ ion spin-freezing transition at around 0.6 K.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our findings, we investigated these methods in a strategic setting and established that, unlike more basic methods such as Dictatorship, both methods produce allocations that are fair up to one good at equilibrium as a necessary condition. Moreover, we altered the analysis of Round-Robin to show that its corresponding game does not have equilibria that are fair up to one good for three specific agents, however, this negative result does not extend to general cases. Furthermore, we explored whether similar efforts can be made to Plaut and Roughgarden's mechanism to

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by high Dice coefficients and fast frame rates, signifies significant potential for its application in medical tool tracking.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the corresponding labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves matching pairs or three-way matches between images, which are difficult to achieve on large datasets due to their computational complexity, especially when dealing with billions of images that typically lack metadata. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel, efficient, and unsupervised learning approach known as large-scale triple-match network (TripleMatchNet), which can effectively learn re-identification representations directly from the large, unlabeled datasets by utilizing contrastive learning on massive datasets. To apply TripleMatchNet, we also introduce three large-scale public datasets containing approximately 1.2 billion images for benchmarking and evaluating re-identification performance under unsupervised conditions. Furthermore, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we also release a Python re-identification matching tool that utilizes TripleMatchNet, known as TROM. Experimental results show superior performance of TripleMatchNet and TROM in various unsupervised evaluation settings, significantly outperforming existing public datasets and state-of-the-art three-way matching models on our three large-scale public datasets.

This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. Results demonstrate the capability of the new framework to achieve competitive accuracy compared to established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is crucial in understanding how planets form. A key factor affecting this process is the wide distribution of protostellar accretion rates at the center of some disks. Research indicates that certain sources with wide accretion rate distributions may be affected by on-off states in their accretion flows. However, confirming this is difficult, particularly with optical monitoring systems that are often used. We analyzed extensive optical and near-infrared datasets, which are among the largest of their kind, in a detailed study. We discovered that some systems, including a previously identified on-off state in the light curves of HH Prf 199, have enormous daily and nightly variations in their mass accretion rates. This implies that some young stars exhibit on-off behavior in their light phases, which may be an on-off state in their accretion flows. This phenomenon is likely caused by magnetospheric interactions, which affect these systems, including XX Cha, in a co-rotation radius that is on the order of 10s of au. This is far outside the disk's inner region, implying that some outer disk structures, such as accreting low-mass mountain waves (AMMWs), may be present far outside of a few au.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information about a specific part of the flag. In this paper, we leverage the geometric properties of the Nakajiki variety to demonstrate that the pushforward of quantum K-theory classes, $K_q^X$, under map $\pi$, can be expressed as a sum of shifted quantum K-theory classes of the target variety $X'$, thereby mirroring the behavior observed in the analogous equivariant setting first identified by R. Tamari.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although the initial approaches based on the Shapley value are conceptually straightforward, the associated computational expenses hinder their scalability to large datasets and real-world machine learning pipelines. The necessity for novel, scalable algorithms for estimating the Shapley value has thus emerged as a critical area of focus in both industry and academia.

We explored possible connections between the number of radio sources observed within 22 galaxy clusters from the MAVERIC survey, and factors like collision rates among stars within those clusters ($\Gamma$) and their masses ($M$). By establishing a threshold for radio signal intensity, we catalogued sources at the heart of the clusters and within areas surrounding the half of their brightness. Our statistical analysis revealed elevated radio activity concentration at the cluster's core compared to its vicinity, yet this activity level didn't correlate with increased collision rates or mass, nor did it vary significantly between clusters near and far, suggesting cosmic distance has no impact on the proportion of radio activity within cluster centers relative to their outskirts. Moreover, we observed distinct collision rate and mass patterns when comparing shallow and steep spectrum radio signals, however this isn't surprising, indicating that collision rate and mass alone aren't sufficient to explain the distribution of radio activity within these clusters, suggesting that additional factors such as magnetic field strength must be considered in our explanation, especially given the known collision-induced radio phenomenon in the Milky Way's core. Ultimately, identifying collisions-induced radio in the Milky Way's globular clusters requires further investigation, including a more detailed examination of their spectral characteristics. Moreover, existing collision rates and masses within the MAVERIC sample suggest collision-induced radio should also be observable within the Milky Way's globular clusters, providing promising leads for future studies with next-generation surveys like the MAVERIC.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in precision-recall performance.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic spacings are measured in terms of wavelength from approximately 0.7 lambda to 0.1 lambda. A comprehensive theoretical framework models thermal alkali metals as groups of interacting radiating dipoles, and demonstrates that photon correlation data can be accurately predicted through random atomic pair positioning. Experiments confirm our findings with positive outcomes. Adjusting key variables within these experiments offers opportunities to investigate distinct regimes of photon behavior.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly eight years has been tracked through various observational methods, including X-ray and optical telemetry. V392 Persei, which orbited its companion in 4.36 hours, was in a stable state before the 2018 eruption, when it observed in the optical spectrum showed it to be a magnetic white dwarf in the range of 0.8 to 1.2 grams per second for the accretion rate and exhibited a 11 to 16 times 10 to the power of 28 erg per second in X-ray emission. V392 Persei, however, rapidly absorbed more matter as the system entered a violent and erratic evolution, ultimately accelerating its evolution into a magnetic white dwarf with a 10 to the power of 34 to 10 to the power of 36 erg per second in X-ray emission. V392 Persei, in addition, was detected in gamma-rays in 2020 with a 3.5 to 8.2 GeV emission which, however, was not observed in 2019, indicating its complex nature and need to be observed with more precision to comprehend its underlying mechanisms. V392 Persei, being a unique and rare example, is not comparable to any

In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for error correction, particularly when combined with stabilizer measurements. Utilizing a single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates in parity-check circuits is demonstrated using the toric code, resulting in improved fault tolerance when applying 4-qubit T-type interactions over sequential two-qubit interactions, according to calculations and visualizations for various noise conditions.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centers of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3, significantly surpassing similar events occurring in globular clusters. Our predictions also reveal that Population III binary black hole binaries might produce nested signals that could be detected by third-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technologies. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays in a network layout. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance signal-to-interference-plus noise ratios, while adhering to constraints on total power, signal symmetry, and power distribution between the transmitters and receivers. By utilizing geometric programming techniques, we seek to develop effective and easily implementable power allocation methods that can improve system performance in a practical and efficient manner.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of 2D systems. In this study, we explore the potential of these topological edge modes for implementing quantum systems. By incorporating two-level atoms into these waveguides, we develop a model known as the Holstein model with time-dependent interactions. Using a numerical approach called KPM, we simulate the system's dynamics and spectral characteristics. Our results reveal that do-si-do solitons can form when an atom is excited, characterized by regions of orientation alignment and disorientation along the waveguide. These structures remain stable over time due to the conservation of excited atom number. Additionally, localized inhibition patterns of energy transfer between atoms emerge, similar to the TIGAR effect. Importantly, the characteristics of these solitons can be controlled by atoms with different chemical potentials. In addition to multi-component solitons, another type of structure known as polaritonic cats can also be generated through coherent superposition of excited states.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used in their creation.
This research presents an optimized version of three widely used text-based game platforms, which we call TextWorldExpress, achieving game simulation speeds of over one million actions per second, around 30 times faster than before.
We show that these improvements largely stem from replacing text-based game code with a highly efficient Python library used in scientific data analysis.
The increased speed in TextWorldExpress enables new possibilities for playing and researching virtual games, notably deep reinforcement learning in large-scale environments.
Interestingly, we observe that traditional learning methods like model-based reinforcement learning and program synthesis struggle to solve these games due to their inadequate games' simulators.
On the other hand, we find that frozen knowledge from real-world knowledge can effectively transfer to these environments, leading to successful results even without extensive fine-tuning.
This research implies that current text-based games might be too hard due to their flawed games' simulators and explores future game designs tailored for modern learning methods while minimizing cheating pathways.

Deep learning models like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have led the field of video recognition, but they come with a price of computationally intensive and inefficient algorithms. Our study presents an innovative solution by re-designing LSTM networks to strike a balance between cutting-edge performance and energy efficiency. By integrating tensor decomposition into the network architecture, we developed a method that minimizes memory access patterns and aligns with the data flow of Field Programmable Gate Array hardware. Introducing a novel, energy-efficient hardware co-design, our algorithm leverages a 3D Tensor Processing Unit, reducing energy consumption by a factor of a hundred compared to traditional GPU-based implementations. By optimizing for energy efficiency rather than pure accuracy, our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art models on several video recognition benchmarks, achieving a remarkable reduction in minimum energy consumption.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach, originally suggested by Cohen and Glazecon, involves the existence of particles with specific squared masses-to-charge ratios. The first contribution of this paper is the demonstration that the first approach can be formulated using the concept of convexity, which is a more fundamental and widely understood principle. The demonstration's second contribution is the introduction of a novel method to establish the convexity of the operator that determines the mass-to-charge ratio, thereby indicating the validity of the weak gravity conjecture. This method may also be applicable in proving the convexity of other operators important in quantum field theory. Furthermore, the paper investigates additional instances of the mass-to-charge ratio operator in quantum field theory and string theory, focusing on the search for particles that contradict the weak gravity conjecture in heterotic $E_8 \times E_8$ theory compactified on $T^6$.

To accelerate quantum simulations for systems with multiple states, we propose a novel method using the quantum imaginary time evolution algorithm in a model space. This approach, we call the model-space quantum imaginary time evolution (MQITE-MS), allows for simultaneous optimization of all states, significantly speeding up convergence and enabling robust convergence even with rough initial guesses. Furthermore, we can speed up quantum simulations by small time steps while maintaining accuracy through a model-space quantum Taylor series evolution (MQTE-MST) algorithm, whose proof lies within our study. The MQITE-MST and MQTE-MST algorithms are especially useful when dealing with strongly correlated systems that exhibit sudden changes in quantum ground states, known as quantum phase transitions, and can also be applied to examine excitation states and their corresponding frequencies, densities, and response functions.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluating electricity market interactions to determine appropriate ancillary services values and quantities proves to be a complex task. In order to address this complexity, we developed an original model called the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM), which utilizes a generalized equilibrium approach to replicate electricity market transformations in response to policy changes. The ASAM model was initially applied to the Italian electricity market, utilizing it to experiment with various scenarios aimed at increasing the provision of frequency regulation services. Specifically, we investigated the impacts of different subsidy and penalty policies on market outcomes, demonstrating how such experiments can assist regulators in designing effective ancillary services provisions. Furthermore, the ASAM model can be integrated with open-source simulation tools like GAMS to support policy analysis and design processes.

A composition of two polynomials equals zero if and only if at least one of the polynomials equals zero for a large subset of prime numbers, where equality in the field of p-adic numbers implies equality everywhere. A composition of n polynomials equals zero infinitely often if and only if the composition of two consecutive polynomials within it satisfies the criterion, as defined by Voloch. However, the structure of Voloch's proof varies significantly between fields of characteristic zero and positive characteristic. This research generalizes the preceding work by two polynomials to polynomials of a higher order in fields of any characteristic. A composition of n polynomials has infinite many zeros if and only if so does the composition of two consecutive polynomials for all possible pairings, with additional requirements imposed by the characteristic of the underlying field. The main characterization holds with multiple necessary and sufficient conditions, with their proof revealing constraints on the factorization of polynomials into components of a specific type, with the count of components following the distribution pattern of floating unipotent matrices over finite fields.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different hypercharges. Our calculations show that these corrections are generally less than one percent of the standard model process but can reach up to several percent in specific parameter space regions. In particular, certain charged scalar configurations can yield larger effects, which could be detectable in future experiments at a lepton collider. Additionally, we considered radiative corrections to the $Zh\gamma\gamma$ process due to new neutral scalars, which are relevant for the IR-safe description of the two-photon process. These corrections are usually less than one percent but can again yield several percent in certain parameter space regions for both the standard and extended scalar sectors. The precise predictions for both processes are crucial for testing the standard model and its potential extensions, which is particularly important for understanding the dark matter sector in scenarios with the Higgs as the weak scale portal to the dark sector.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a mass-critical regime. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse in a finite time, regardless of their initial energy. Our result, achieved through a combination of barrier techniques and model problems, provides a purely geometric method with respect to the obstacle for an infinite set of blow-up solutions. Our approach overcomes limitations of previous studies by extending applicable domains from star-shaped obstacles to those with intricate boundaries and by utilizing a variational method capable of handling high-dimensional problems. Our theorem makes significant contributions to the field by offering the first examples of blow-up solutions in a mass supercritical regime outside a compact convex obstacle and thus, represents a major advancement in the field.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of strong correlations systems, as observed in V$_2$O$_3$.  Our data suggest a major influence of electron-phonon coupling on the metal-insulator transition, with Raman spectroscopy revealing significant changes in the frequency and intensity of the phonon mode associated with the trimerization of oxygen atoms across the metal-insulator transition, which showed increased frequency but decreased intensity after the transition,  a consequence possibly of altered screening and electron-phon

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearisation is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, crystallographic, and atomic properties. However, traditional methods require retrieving both the amplitude and phase of scattered light. We propose a reverse approach, where the sample is designed to emit light in a specific pattern, effectively controlling the phase of light, which is then detected using coherent x-ray scattering. This method, known as phase retrieval spectroscopy, is demonstrated by applying it to examine the dynamics of charge ordering in manganites.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram of the corresponding classical spin model and apply a finite-size scaling analysis. This analysis helps determine the existence of dynamic critical points, a phenomenon observed in time-series systems showing abrupt changes near critical transitions. We map out the dynamic critical points in the model's parameter space. These findings have direct implications for assessing the performance of quantum error correcting codes in the face of realistic errors, as demonstrated with the quantum repetition code. Specifically, we determine the fundamental threshold for errors parallel to the logical qubit and the threshold for diagonal errors, both of which are crucial for evaluating code efficiency.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In our study, three tellurene monolayers with rock-salt topology were found to be unusually stable when combined with organic functionalization in the form of -NH2, -NO2, and -CH3 groups or in isolation as bare tellurene. We examined the strain-induced phase transitions and defect formation energies to validate the structural stability of these devices. We discovered that tellurene with -NH2, -NO2, and -CH3 groups or bare tellurene exhibit large in-gap values of 1.17 eV, 0.9 eV, and 0.47 eV, and 0.29 eV respectively which distinguish them from black phosphorene and magadiite. Furthermore, all these devices displayed significant quantum spin Hall edge conductance and large in-gap time-reversal symmetry-breaking gaps when subjected to exchange magnetization, making them ideal candidates for developing 2D topological insulators.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases.
