Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion in rotating stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the identification of multiple signal features. Traditional search methods fall short in extracting rich information due to their lower resolution and reliability. We introduce novel deep learning techniques for both detecting and classifying gravitational waves from neutron star-black hole mergers. Our approaches, employing only a few thousand training samples, yield superior performance in this merging parameter space compared to their nearest counterparts. We demonstrate that our detector can identify region-specific prominent features in the 2D morphological signal space, enabling better analysis of the merging waves and potentially providing insights into the underlying physics of these events.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many healthcare institutions still fail to track and link essential social data with clinical care due to the labor-intensive nature of the process and the diversity of data entry formats. In order to automate this process, using natural language processing to extract social data from unstructured clinical notes has gained significant interest in recent years. However, the existence of existing NLP models' output in the form of named entity recognition (NER) or dependency parsing led to the creation of a multi-stage system leveraging neural networks and a marker-based approach, which proved to outperform existing models by 10% in F1-score when evaluated with 10 different social determinants of health data types.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the central star could be represented as "episodic accretion," a process previously thought to be one-dimensional. However, the strong outflows generated by the central star can be redirected or blocked by the surrounding disk, thus allowing episodic accretion to proceed unimpeded. Similarly, interactions with the disk's viscous process also tend to allow the central star to absorb objects without suffering one-dimensional conflicts. When considering the competition between accretion and further fragmentation, it becomes clear that most objects will be accreted due to their larger mass compared to small particles that may be ejected into the outflows. When it comes to mass accumulation, simulations reveal that small amounts of matter may be added through accretion and mergers but a sudden, large event, such as the accretion of a star forming clump, may significantly add to the star's mass. To better explain observed correlations, it is suggested that clumps of matter should be included in the simulations. When comparing simulated stars to observed clumps, the former appear less evolved due to the presence of surrounding clumps, thus suggesting that observed clumps may actually represent multiple stars or star systems.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets, one of which is closely related to Buchholz-Lechner-Summers' chiral CFT deformation. We've also successfully isolated the strictly local elements in another instance. Furthermore, using endomorphisms on the U(1)-current net and the free fermion net developed by Longo-Witten, we've constructed a large family of wedge-local nets.

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, adolescents, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. This methodology is then applied to two real-world case studies. Findings indicate that as 5G adoption increases, so too will the exposure from 5G cellular towers. However, international safety guidelines still remain unaffected by these findings. Interestingly, children's and teenagers' exposure rates to 5G resemble those of adults, while exposure within schools and medical centers is lower due to their layout and operating features. Furthermore, total 5G exposure found to be significantly lower than pre-5G exposure.

This study investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We seek out an infinite depth scenario and employ the Dysthe equation, modified to account for the presence of constant vorticity. By utilizing a Hamiltonian formulation for the Dysthe equation with vorticity, we derive a new symmetry property and prove the conservation of a specific norm. Additionally, we derive a new identity for the surface waves and perform numerical simulations to assess their accuracy, which reveal our results converge to the exact solutions as the equation's parameters increase. We also derive an infinite depth Dysthe equation with vorticity and demonstrate that our results hold true even in this modified scenario.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of processing sonar data in real-time through a non-linear filter, this method offers a flexible alternative to complex sensor setups often hindered by weather and surface obstructions. By utilizing a simple sonar sensor, whether it's one in number or multiple, and leveraging the modular nature of the layered control system, we can achieve seamless navigation and obstacle avoidance. We delve into the design of this approach, present its theoretical underpinnings, and illustrate its practical application through real-world testing, consistently yielding stable and smooth indoor navigation results.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative proximal gradient method to solve it. Notably, the proposed approach achieves an optimal convergence rate, producing a series of approximate solutions that gradually align with the highest density line within a finite number of iterations. This theory is validated through numerical experiments.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski enhanced earlier work by investigating how to approximate winning strategies in finite-valued energy games using totally ordered groups. This paper builds upon their study by extending the framework to include order-type $\tau$ within the domain of totally ordered groups, particularly those of prime height one. The work retains the height restrictions while removing the necessity for archimedean properties, thereby contributing a more general theory to the field.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy and specific heat. By adjusting the chemical potential, we can potentially enhance the magnetically induced heat effect. Notably, Rashba coupling has negligible impact on the MCE. Additionally, we observe giant peak values in entropy and specific heat at intervalley points in the Brillouin zone, which can be harnessed for efficient waste-heat recovery via the MCE in 2D materials.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' Feynman diagrams can be used to determine the preamplitude, from which the amplitude at any radial position in the conformal finite region can be recovered. In the limit of large masses, this approach yields a consistent agreement with reduced transplanar box diagrams obtained through an melon expansion, thus validating the analysis. The construction method provides a foundation for extending calculations to higher-loop levels and can potentially be adapted for calculating three-loop amplitudes, as illustrated by the flow of a three-loop melon diagram. The research findings are carried out using $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity in AdS five times S$^5$, though most of the steps can be modified to analyze three-loop four point amplitude calculations for type IIB supergravity in the same space. The research can also be adapted to investigate calculations at the same loop level for N=4 supergravity in AdS five times S$^5$ using zigzag graphs in their original form as well as by employing a four-dimensional partial amplitude construction at three loops involving two zigzag diagrams along with an 844 pentagon box. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a dynamic data layout management system that minimizes memory fragmentation.  In evaluation tests, DynaSOAr outperformed a widely-used C++ object-oriented programming library (CGL) and a static allocation GPU framework (GROOVE) in terms of execution speed and memory management efficiency.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr demonstrated a significant performance improvement, achieving up to 2.6 times better runtime performance and 5.6 times less external memory spillover in a case study involving a graph degree computation algorithm.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse whose frequency increases over time as it moves through the target. We discovered that a shorter high-frequency component of the pulse triggers self-induced transparency within the target, allowing the pulse to move through a plasma window while surrounding parts of the pulse are reflected. As a result, the high-frequency component of the pulse produces a stronger current than the lower-frequency component, due to the differences in their self-induced transparency periods. This current, composed of particles moving at various speeds, can be controlled by adjusting the pulse's chirp rate, thus influencing the acceleration of ions. Simulations showed that this effect holds up to intense intensities of $10^{21} W/m^2$ in a $120 fs$ pulse and can occur with existing commercial pulses.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age of approximately 400 million years. Additionally, they determined that it resembles the well-studied sun and lies at a distance of 146 light-years from Earth, in the direction of the Perseus constellation. Three of the planets, TOI-712 b, c, and d, are referred to as the "adolescent mini-Neptune trio," due to their young age and intermediate masses. They are situated in the formationally sensitive middle range of periods, between super-Earths and hot Jupiters. There's also a third-transit signal in the system, a rare phenomenon globally. By analyzing the mass of the stellar system, the team found that TOI-712 e, a rocky planet, orbits in about 11.6 days and has a temperature of approximately $430$ K, making it potentially located in or near the habitable zone of the star.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds.  Moreover, both CO and NO molecules within these SC or SN structures lie external to the TiO2 surface. The total energy differences between various SC or SN structures are calculated, and carbon oxidation states are determined to be +4 in EC SN structures, in contrast to IN SC structures where carbon oxidation states are either +2 or +4, depending on whether the structure is magnetic or non-magnetic.  To further validate our calculations, we compared our theoretical oxidation states with those derived from PBE0

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy. X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzing these quantities, measurements are constrained by instrumental uncertainties and the inherent variability in cosmic observations. Here, the formalism established in a previous paper is expanded to account for the statistical uncertainty in line diagnostics, specifically structure functions. Statistical variance contributes to total variance in several ways, influenced by the detector's geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of turbulent fields. These terms hold significant importance for studying turbulence at smaller scales. A demonstration is conducted for the X-IFU using a simulated turbulent velocity map of a galaxy cluster similar to Coma. Results indicate excellent agreement with theoretical formulas for structure function estimation and its associated variance. These derived expressions can be applied to any X-ray measurement of turbulent structure functions and provide a framework for optimizing future instrumentation and observational strategies.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation in the sky. Within this region, numerous dense gas clusters exhibit anisotropic spatial distributions. To investigate the geometric configurations of these dense gas clusters, a 2D correlation function is employed in this study. Utilizing data from the Azimuthal Dense gas Survey (AZDS), a total of 446 dense gas clusters in the CMZ are analyzed. When comparing the orientations of these clusters to a previously modeled magnetic field in the SMZ, a notable agreement is found for the majority of regions. To further investigate, a new method based on a tensor is introduced to characterize the dense gas clusters anisotropy, providing descriptive parameters such as an anisotropic ellipsoid and principal component analysis. These results suggest that the dense gas clusters anisotropy in the CMZ can be effectively quantified through the 2D correlation function.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centric system offers enhanced efficiency and user-friendliness when compared to conventional methods.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Our simulations indicate that interacting linearly polarized lasers with thin metal targets yields a dense stream of spin-aligned positrons in three dimensions. Utilizing an intense laser at 800 nm with 10<sup>22</sup> W/cm<sup>2</sup> intensity and thin nickel or copper targets of 125-1000 MeV, we can produce a dense flux of spin-aligned positrons in three dimensions. In comparison to traditional radiation thrust methods, our proposed technique results in nearly a two-fold increase in positron density and a substantial reduction in ratio of total charge to positron alignment ratio by a factor of over 10.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This work introduces a fully integrated, low-power temperature sensor suitable for battery-operated systems. The sensor's block diagram, simulation results, and detailed design parameters are presented. It utilizes a PTAT voltage-based conversion method, featuring an 11-bit ADC for high-resolution readings. The sensor's 0.6V$-$1.8V power supply range ensures versatility across various systems. It achieves 0.24{\deg}C resolution and 1.06nJ per conversion energy at 1.35V with a 10kHz frequency. The sensor's design includes a 140k$\Omega$ equivalent output impedance, enabling seamless integration with on-chip readers.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming key features of previous simulations. In configurations resembling the twisted torus, our simulations demonstrated the development of stable turbulent motions in the equatorial plane, while maintaining order in the magnetic fields during periods of intense turbulence. Additionally, these configurations are resistant to the development of instability induced by the magnetic Reynolds number.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group dynamics, including understanding how the emergence of infrared modes influences the evolution of the effective action. We explore the applicability of our framework to standard models and complex systems, while also exploring its potential for uncovering new insights into quantum field theories that might elude perturbative analysis.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on general-purpose video platform metasearch tools like Google, YouTube, and Facebook to find specific music. These tools, however, lack a tagged-based system that enables users to input a song and receive related tracks. Proposed solution to this limitation is a music-oriented metasearch platform called Pied Piper, which provides a more efficient method for discovering music via web page searches. Additionally, we introduce a Parrot module that utilizes the Pinterest API to generate a set of related songs based on the original music title.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04451, arXiv:2103.04452, arXiv:2103.04453, arXiv:2103.04454], the study establishes connections between underlying stacks and Lie groupoids through equivalence relations. Key concepts such as connections, curvatures, and horizontal lifts for connections are defined within the framework of principal bundles over these structures. Notably, the studies establish the concept of differential forms adapted to these bundles and introduce connections that mirror the characteristics of a corresponding underlying differential equation, thereby establishing a parallel to the corresponding stack of a Lie algebra equiation.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each individual point significantly enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine scalable techniques for handling large datasets. Ultimately, our team's top classifier achieves remarkable precision-recall levels of 0.99 for identifying trees and 0.96 for identifying buildings when using LEI features and the random forest algorithm on a substantial dataset consisting of approximately one hundred and five million points.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and reliability have been significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings. The current methods can still distinguish the hypothesis of UHECR and neutrino large-scale correlation from no correlation with a minimum statistical significance of 4.5 sigma, and the data support a correlated universe up to 30 degrees separation, 12 degrees, or 3 years look-back time with a minimum statistical significance of 3.9 sigma.
